questions.q: Structurally, how does a Kubernetes Secret compare to a ConfigMap?
options: They are completely different objects with no shared structure
A Secret is nearly identical in structure to a ConfigMap (key-value data, consumed via env or volume), but intended for sensitive data
A Secret can only be consumed as a volume mount, never as an environment variable
A Secret automatically encrypts its values while a ConfigMap cannot store strings at all
questions.explain: Secrets and ConfigMaps share nearly the same shape and consumption patterns (env vars or volume mounts) — the difference is intent and some built-in handling, not basic structure.

questions.q: Why is it incorrect to say a Kubernetes Secret is 'encrypted'?
options: Secrets are stored as encrypted by default; this statement is actually true
By default, Secret values are only base64-encoded, which is trivially reversible — real encryption at rest requires explicit cluster configuration
Secrets cannot store string values, only binary data
Secrets are stored exclusively in the Pod's memory, never on disk
questions.explain: Base64 is an encoding, not encryption — anyone with read access can decode it instantly. Actual encryption at rest in etcd is an opt-in cluster-level configuration, not Kubernetes's default behavior.

questions.q: In a Secret manifest, what is the difference between stringData and data?
options: data is for plain text; stringData is for already-encoded values
stringData accepts plain text and Kubernetes base64-encodes it automatically; data expects values that are already base64-encoded
They are interchangeable with no functional difference
stringData only works with type: kubernetes.io/tls
questions.explain: stringData lets you write plain text and Kubernetes handles the base64 encoding for storage; data requires the caller to supply already base64-encoded values.

questions.q: Which Secret type would Northbridge use to let a Pod pull its image from a private container registry?
options: Opaque
kubernetes.io/tls
kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson, referenced via imagePullSecrets
kubernetes.io/basic-auth
questions.explain: kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson holds private registry credentials, and a Pod references it via spec.imagePullSecrets to authenticate when pulling its image.

questions.q: Why might mounting a Secret as a volume be preferred over injecting it as an environment variable for a highly sensitive value?
options: Environment variables cannot be used with Secrets at all
Volume-mounted Secrets are automatically encrypted while environment variables never are
Environment variables can leak more easily — through crash dumps, child-process inheritance, or introspection — so a mounted file is often the safer consumption method
Mounting as a volume is required by the Kubernetes API for all Secrets
questions.explain: Both methods expose the same underlying data, but environment variables have more common leak paths (crash dumps, subprocess inheritance, etc.), so mounting as a file is often considered the safer option for sensitive values.
